How to build a real SaaS with AI, from zero How to build a real SaaS with AI, from zero: a website that sells it, logins, a database, monthly payments and photos, all built by talking to Claude Code. I never wrote a line of code. The example: MenuTap, a $9/month QR menu app for cafés. 1. The tool: Claude Code inside VS Code (the extension), a paid Claude plan, an empty folder. 2. The plan: "Interview me about it, then write the CLAUDE.md." Tell it you've never coded and it picks the tools for you. 3. The website: home, pricing and sign-up. The first draft looked like every AI site, so: the free frontend-design plugin + "make it look premium" + 6 AI photos. 4. The database: Supabase, running on your own computer first. Publishable key in the browser, secret key only on the server. 5. The rule: anyone can read a published menu, only the owner can edit it. Put it in the database, then make the AI prove it with a second owner. It tried 24 ways. All failed. 6. Customer side: the public menu + a QR code that holds a permanent link. 7. Payments: a Stripe sandbox, $9/month, a webhook unlocks the account. 4242 unlocks, the decline card stays locked, fake "she paid" messages get refused. 8. Photos, then a security review before launch: nothing critical, 13 real problems, 11 fixed. 9. Online: GitHub (private), Vercel (Pro, because taking payments is commercial use), the online Supabase project, your domain. Your first AI agent doesn’t need to run your business. It needs to take one annoying task off your plate. When people ask me where to start with AI agents, they usually expect a tool recommendation. My answer is almost always a question: what’s the task you’d happily never do again? For me, it was filing meeting notes. Not glamorous, but it came up every week, followed the same pattern, and quietly ate time I could have spent with clients. The part most tutorials skip is the boring middle. Writing out the process like you’re onboarding a new hire, deciding what the agent should never do, and testing it on real examples before you trust it on its own. That’s where agents either become useful or get abandoned after a week. Start small. One task, one hour back every week. That’s a real win.
